opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that our decision to open up the Cosmos world foundation models didn't come *from* DeepSeek. We'd been planning it for a long time, and we announced it around CES, right before the big DeepSeek moment. But I do see the two as part of the same current, and DeepSeek reinforced a lot of what we believed.

Our reasoning was simple. Physical AI is still very early. In language models, the community had years of open models, datasets, and benchmarks before things really took off. For robotics and autonomous driving, we don't have that yet. Every lab and startup builds its own simulator, collects its own data, and trains its own world model from scratch. That's hugely wasteful. If we want a "ChatGPT moment" for robotics, someone has to provide a strong foundation that people can fine-tune, post-train, and build on. NVIDIA is in a good position to do that because we have the compute and the data pipeline, and frankly our business does better when the whole ecosystem grows.

What DeepSeek showed the world, and I think this was very important, is that open weights plus a clear technical report can move the entire field fast. People could reproduce it, poke at it, improve it, and suddenly ideas spread in weeks instead of years. It also showed that openness isn't just charity. It builds trust, attracts talent, and makes your work the default starting point. That validated our bet. It made it much easier internally and externally to explain why we should keep releasing models, tokenizers, data curation tools, and keep being transparent about how we trained them.

There's also a difference worth noting. With language, the internet already gave everyone a huge shared dataset. In physical AI, data is the bottleneck. Real-world robot data is expensive, and it's scattered. So for us, open-sourcing a world model is also a way to give people a data engine. You can generate synthetic experiences, test policies, and explore scenarios you can't easily capture in reality.

So I'd put it like this. DeepSeek didn't change our direction, but it changed the atmosphere. It made everyone realize open models can be frontier models. For physical AI, I believe the field will only mature if it's open, and we want to help make that happen.

r001.rationale: The response says the decision had been planned for a long time and “didn't come from DeepSeek,” which it says reinforced the existing direction.

r002.rationale: It describes releasing a foundation for robotics labs and startups to build on, and says NVIDIA benefits when the physical AI ecosystem grows.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think people sometimes connect those two things more tightly than they really were. When we started Cosmos, the decision to open it was already made. Our thinking was pretty simple: physical AI is a much bigger problem than any one company can solve. You need the robotics companies, the autonomous driving companies, the academic labs, all building on the same foundation, and you can't get that if the foundation is locked behind an API. NVIDIA's business is the platform. If more people build physical AI, more people need our compute. So open-sourcing the world foundation models was aligned with our interests from day one, not something we had to be pushed into.

That said, I'd be lying if I said DeepSeek had no effect. What DeepSeek showed very clearly was that open models can be at the frontier, and that the community will adopt them extremely fast when they are. That changed the conversation internally in a good way. It made it easier to argue for releasing not just the weights, but also the training recipes, the data curation pipeline, the tokenizers, the whole stack. Because the lesson from DeepSeek was that the openness itself creates the momentum. People read the paper, they reproduce it, they improve on it, and suddenly your approach becomes the default.

I also think there's a certain respect I have for the engineering culture there. They did a lot with constrained resources, and they wrote everything down. For physical AI, where data is the bottleneck more than compute, that mindset of being transparent about how you built things is exactly what the field needs. So I'd say DeepSeek didn't cause our decision, but it validated it, and it probably accelerated how far we were willing to go.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the decision to open Cosmos had already been made and that DeepSeek did not cause it, though DeepSeek later validated and accelerated the scope of openness.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes opening the foundation so robotics and autonomous driving companies can build on it, and says broader physical AI adoption supports NVIDIA’s platform business.

The motivation is to help people build on a shared foundation. Physical AI involves many different environments, robots, and applications, and no single team can cover all of them. Making the work available lets researchers and developers experiment, contribute, and move the field forward together.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate those two things a little. DeepSeek has certainly brought more attention to what open models can enable, but I wouldn’t describe our decision to open-source physical AI work as a response to DeepSeek. The motivation is that physical AI is too broad for one company to solve alone. You need researchers, robotics companies, and developers working on different parts of the problem.

By sharing models and tools, we give people a starting point they can inspect, adapt, and build on. DeepSeek’s influence reinforces the value of that approach, but I’d be careful about claiming it caused the decision.
